thread.title: The Big Sector Shakeup Is About to Hit the Stock Market. Blink and You Might Miss It

author: Evie Liu
title: The Big Sector Shakeup Is About to Hit the Stock Market. Blink and You Might Miss It
text:
Illustration: rawpixel By Evie Liu Updated Sept. 21, 2018 3:53 p.m. ET Stocks such as Facebook (FB), Netflix (NFLX), and Verizon Communications (VZ) will live under the same roof from next week on. The Global Industry Classification Standard , or the GICS, is creating a new sector called Communication Services, which will absorb names from the old tech, consumer discretionary, and telecom sectors.
GICS is a standardized classification system for stocks developed by S&P Global and MSCI in 1999. S&P Global will incorporate the latest changes at the close on Friday, Sep. 21, while MSCI will do the same on Nov. 30.
Alphabet and Facebook will no longer be part of the tech sector once S&P and MSCI change the way they classify companies. Within the S&P 500, six stocks from Information Technology, 13 from Consumer Discretionary, and three from Telecommunication Services will be moved into the new Communication Services sector. The reclassified stocks include some of the biggest names in the market: Alphabet (GOOGL), Facebook, Twitter (TWTR), Netflix, Walt Disney (DIS), Comcast (CMCSA), AT&T (T), and Verizon.
Read more : A Market Shakeup Is Pushing Alphabet and Facebook Out of the Tech Sector
About a tenth of the S&P 500’s market capitalization will be affected by the change, Wells Fargo analyst Christopher Harvey estimates in a report published Friday. The new Communication Services sector will account for about 10% of the S&P 500’s market cap while Information Technology will drop to roughly 20% from the current 26%, and Consumer Discretionary will decline to about 10% from 13%.
The sector changes are likely to have a limited impact for most “long only” active asset managers, says Harvey, as many of them already have internal stock grouping system that might be more relevant and timely.
Most impacted by the reclassification will be sector ETFs that are benchmarked against the GICS indexes, among which State Street and Vanguard’s sector funds.
While Vanguard already started its transition process a few months ago, the SPDR sector ETFs will institute their changes at the close on Sept 21, 2018. The Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK), with about $27 billion in assets, and Consumer Discretionary Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLY), with $18 billion, will sell out their holdings of the stocks moving into the Communication Services sector. On the other hand, there will be inflows for the rest of tech and discretionary companies in order to fill up the gap. Ryan Talbot from Instinet wrote in a report that he expects around $20 billion of rebalance flows for the two funds.
The reclassification would cause some liquidity demands for the affected stocks in XLK and XLY, but likely minimal. As calculated by Harvey, the liquidity demand created by the GICS flows will be smaller than the average daily volume for most of the affected stocks.
Harvey also pointed out that Friday, Sep. 21, is also the day when S&P does its quarterly index rebalance, which will influence the fund flows, as well. For example, the XLK would add more Apple (AAPL) shares to fill the gap left by Alphabet and Facebook, but also need to reduce the stock’s weighting due to the overall S&P 500 rebalance. Talbot of Instinet estimates that about half of the GICS flows will be balanced out by the S&P quarterly rebalance flows.
As ETFs gear up for the rebalance, investors are also adjusting their sector exposure—some before the rebalance, while some plan to afterwards. Since the repositioning is spread out over months and not a one-off event, the impact shouldn’t be too dramatic, writes Talbot.
State Street has also launched the Communication Services Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLC) back in June. The fund hasn’t gathered a huge amount of assets yet, but Talbot noted that creation activity has started to pick up.
